results.question: What is a reticulocyte count and why is it ordered?
results.answer:
A reticulocyte count measures the number of reticulocytes (immature red blood cells) in the blood [c001]. Reticulocytes are produced in the bone marrow and mature into red blood cells within one to two days [c001].

- A reticulocyte count is ordered when other blood tests show abnormal red blood cell levels, such as a complete blood count, hemoglobin test, or hematocrit test [c001].

- An abnormal reticulocyte count can indicate serious health conditions including anemia and conditions of the bone marrow, liver, and kidneys [c001].

- A higher-than-normal reticulocyte count may indicate new or ongoing bleeding with the body producing more red blood cells to replace losses, or in newborns, hemolytic disease of the newborn [c001].

- A lower-than-normal reticulocyte count may indicate pernicious anemia, a type of megaloblastic anemia that occurs when the body is not getting enough B vitamins (B12 and folate) or cannot absorb them adequately [c001].

Reference only — always follow your facility's policies and verify with your provider.
evidence:
[c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) A reticulocyte count (retic count) measures the number of reticulocytes in your blood. Reticulocytes are immature (still developing) red blood cells (RBCs). Your body makes reticulocytes in your bone marrow. Then it sends them into your blood, where they mature into red blood cells within one to two days. The main job of the red blood cells is to move oxygen from your lungs to every cell in your body.
[c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) If the reticulocyte count is too high or too low, it can be a sign of a serious health condition, including anemia and conditions of the bone marrow, liver, and kidneys.
[c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) Other names: retic count, reticulocyte percent, reticulocyte index, corrected reticulocyte, reticulocyte production index, RPI

[c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) Sometimes newborn babies may have a reticulocyte count test to check for a blood disorder called hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). This condition may happen if your blood does not match the blood type of your unborn baby. This is known as Rh incompatibility. It causes your immune system to attack your baby's red blood cells.

[c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) There is very little risk to your baby with a needle stick test. [c001] (source: Reticulocyte Count; publisher: National Library of Medicine — MedlinePlus; retrieved 2026-09-17) To understand the results of a reticulocyte count test, your provider will consider your symptoms, medical history, and the results of other blood tests.
